keyVerseText: Terrors shall make him afraid on every side, and shall drive him to his feet. drive: Heb. scatter
rootMeaning: The root of בַּלָּהָה (ballâhâh) is בָּלַהּ (bâlahh), which conveys the idea of trouble or a palpitation, often implying a trembling or fearful agitation. This root meaning highlights an experience of intense disturbance or alarm, which in its causative form can mean to terrify. Thus, beyond the common English glosses of 'terror' or 'calamity,' the root suggests a visceral, almost physical reaction to overwhelming distress or fear.
usageInScripture: The word בַּלָּהָה appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, consistently conveying a sense of terror, calamity, or destruction. It is translated variously as 'terrors,' 'trouble,' or 'calamity,' reflecting a range from personal fear to widespread disaster. The plural form often emphasizes multiple or ongoing terrors, underscoring the pervasive nature of the dread or destruction described. This consistency in usage reveals the word's strong association with divine judgment or overwhelming adversity.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding בַּלָּהָה in its original language enriches our grasp of the biblical portrayal of human frailty and God's righteous judgment. The term captures not just external calamities but the internal terror that accompanies separation from God's protection. For believers, it underscores the reality of spiritual warfare and the consequences of sin, while also pointing toward the comfort found in God's sovereignty over all terror and destruction. Christ's victory ultimately conquers these terrors, offering peace amid the calamities that this word so vividly describes.
keyVerseReflection: In Job 18:11, 'Terrors shall make him afraid on every side, and shall drive him to his feet,' the word בַּלָּהָה conveys an overwhelming fear that surrounds and unsettles a person completely. The use of 'terrors' here intensifies the image of being besieged by frightening forces, illustrating the profound distress that leads to a loss of stability. This highlights the human experience of being overwhelmed by calamity, a condition from which only God's deliverance can truly rescue.
